claim: The cytomatrix at the active zone (CAZ) is a macromolecular complex that facilitates the supply of release-ready synaptic vesicles to support neurotransmitter release at synapses.
source: The cytomatrix at the active zone (CAZ) is a macromolecular complex that facilitates the supply of release-ready synaptic vesicles to support neurotransmitter release at synapses.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about the CAZ and its role in synaptic transmission.

claim: The synaptic ribbon serves a dual function as a conduit for diffusion of synaptic vesicles and a platform for vesicles to fuse distal to the plasma membrane itself, via compound fusion.
source: We find that the synaptic ribbon serves a dual function as a conduit for diffusion of synaptic vesicles and a platform for vesicles to fuse distal to the plasma membrane itself, via compound fusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from super-resolution imaging of single vesicles and pHluorin fusion events presented in the manuscript.

claim: The combination of diffusion and compound fusion functions allows the ribbon-type CAZ to achieve the continuous transmitter release required by synapses of neurons that carry tonic, graded visual signals in the retina.
source: The combination of these functions allows the ribbon-type CAZ to achieve the continuous transmitter release required by synapses of neurons that carry tonic, graded visual signals in the retina.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed dual functions of the ribbon and the known physiological requirements of retinal bipolar neurons.

claim: The CAZ is thought to capture and organize synaptic vesicles to support neurotransmitter release by presynaptic terminals.
source: A macromolecular complex, the cytomatrix at the active zone (CAZ; Südhof, 2012) is thought to capture and organize synaptic vesicles to support neurotransmitter release by presynaptic terminals (Sigrist and Schmitz, 2011; Gundelfinger and Fijtova, 2012; Hallermann and Silver, 2013), but the dynamics of this process at living synapses remain largely elusive.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on the CAZ.

claim: The dynamics of vesicle capture and organization at the CAZ in living synapses remain largely elusive.
source: A macromolecular complex, the cytomatrix at the active zone (CAZ; Südhof, 2012) is thought to capture and organize synaptic vesicles to support neurotransmitter release by presynaptic terminals (Sigrist and Schmitz, 2011; Gundelfinger and Fijtova, 2012; Hallermann and Silver, 2013), but the dynamics of this process at living synapses remain largely elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: Fluorescent Ribeye-binding peptide (RBP) marks the synaptic ribbon found at the active zones of retinal bipolar cells.
source: To label the living active zone, we used fluorescent Ribeye-binding peptide (RBP; Zenisek et al., 2004), which marks the synaptic ribbon found at the active zones of retinal bipolar cells (BPCs) and other neurons that release neurotransmitter continuously in response to graded changes in membrane potential (Matthews and Fuchs, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and is used as a method in this study.

claim: Retinal bipolar cells and other neurons with synaptic ribbons release neurotransmitter continuously in response to graded changes in membrane potential.
source: To label the living active zone, we used fluorescent Ribeye-binding peptide (RBP; Zenisek et al., 2004), which marks the synaptic ribbon found at the active zones of retinal bipolar cells (BPCs) and other neurons that release neurotransmitter continuously in response to graded changes in membrane potential (Matthews and Fuchs, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on ribbon synapse physiology.

claim: Synaptic vesicles are 30–50 nm in diameter.
source: However, monitoring the trafficking of tiny synaptic vesicles (30–50 nm in diameter) is a technical challenge, which we were able to meet by targeting a photoactivatable fluorescent protein to synaptic vesicles and using super-resolution photoactivated localization microscopy (Betzig et al., 2006) to track movements of single vesicles in voltage-clamped synaptic terminals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about synaptic vesicle size.

claim: Photoactivated localization microscopy can be used to track movements of single vesicles in voltage-clamped synaptic terminals.
source: However, monitoring the trafficking of tiny synaptic vesicles (30–50 nm in diameter) is a technical challenge, which we were able to meet by targeting a photoactivatable fluorescent protein to synaptic vesicles and using super-resolution photoactivated localization microscopy (Betzig et al., 2006) to track movements of single vesicles in voltage-clamped synaptic terminals.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the PALM technique and demonstrated by data in this study.

claim: pHluorin can be targeted to synaptic vesicles to detect vesicle fusion.
source: We also targeted the exocytosis reporter pHluorin (Sankaranarayanan et al., 2000) to synaptic vesicles (Granseth et al., 2006; Voglmaier et al., 2006) in order to detect vesicle fusion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and demonstrated by data in this study.

claim: Previous studies of synaptic vesicle trafficking at ribbon synapses of BPCs have been carried out using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy (TIRFM) to image single vesicles labeled with FM dye.
source: Previously, studies of synaptic vesicle trafficking and fusion at ribbon synapses of BPCs have been carried out using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy (TIRFM) to image single vesicles labeled with FM dye (Zenisek et al., 2000, 2002; Holt et al., 2004; Midorikawa et al., 2007; Zenisek, 2008; Joselevitch and Zenisek, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous TIRFM studies.

claim: Vesicles stably associate with ribbons in the absence of stimulation ('residents').
source: Some of the conclusions from this work are: 1) vesicles stably associate with ribbons in the absence of stimulation ('residents'), 2) these resident vesicles rapidly undergo exocytosis in response to depolarization, and 3) new vesicles ('newcomers') appear, move toward the membrane, and fuse during sustained depolarization.
evidence: This is a conclusion from previous TIRFM studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Resident vesicles rapidly undergo exocytosis in response to depolarization.
source: Some of the conclusions from this work are: 1) vesicles stably associate with ribbons in the absence of stimulation ('residents'), 2) these resident vesicles rapidly undergo exocytosis in response to depolarization, and 3) new vesicles ('newcomers') appear, move toward the membrane, and fuse during sustained depolarization.
evidence: This is a conclusion from previous TIRFM studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: New vesicles ('newcomers') appear, move toward the membrane, and fuse during sustained depolarization.
source: Some of the conclusions from this work are: 1) vesicles stably associate with ribbons in the absence of stimulation ('residents'), 2) these resident vesicles rapidly undergo exocytosis in response to depolarization, and 3) new vesicles ('newcomers') appear, move toward the membrane, and fuse during sustained depolarization.
evidence: This is a conclusion from previous TIRFM studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: TIRFM is limited to imaging labeled vesicles within ~100 nm of the plasma membrane.
source: Although TIRFM is a powerful approach to study membrane-associated phenomena, it is limited to imaging labeled vesicles within ~100 nm of the plasma membrane (e.g., Zenisek et al., 2000), which is insufficient to provide coverage of all the ribbon-associated vesicles.
evidence: This is a known limitation of TIRFM supported by citation.

claim: TIRFM requires tight adherence of the plasma membrane to a planar substrate, which restricts observations to a small part of the terminal and eliminates the natural membrane curvature in that observable region.
source: The method also requires tight adherence of the plasma membrane to a planar substrate, which restricts observations to a small part of the terminal and eliminates the natural membrane curvature in that observable region.
evidence: This is a known limitation of TIRFM based on the physical requirements of the technique.

claim: Only Midorikawa et al. (2007) and Zenisek (2008) have combined vesicle imaging with ribbon labeling in previous TIRFM studies.
source: Furthermore, to our knowledge, only Midorikawa et al. (2007) and Zenisek (2008) have combined vesicle imaging with ribbon labeling, and then only in sequentially acquired images separated by some time, which were intended to test whether observed hotspots of fusion coincided with ribbons.
evidence: This is a statement about the literature supported by specific citations.

claim: Two-color laser scanning methods allow single labeled vesicles to be observed throughout the full extent of the ribbon in voltage-clamped synaptic terminals.
source: Because of these limitations, we used two-color laser scanning methods that allowed single labeled vesicles to be observed throughout the full extent of the ribbon in voltage-clamped synaptic terminals, while the ribbon and cell border were imaged with a second fluorescent label.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The positions of the ribbon and a labeled vesicle can be known accurately using the two-color laser scanning method.
source: Since the positions of the ribbon and a labeled vesicle were known accurately, we were able to detect vesicle movements on the ribbon prior to fusion and determine where vesicles resided on the ribbon when they fused.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Vesicle movements on the ribbon prior to fusion can be detected using the two-color laser scanning method.
source: Since the positions of the ribbon and a labeled vesicle were known accurately, we were able to detect vesicle movements on the ribbon prior to fusion and determine where vesicles resided on the ribbon when they fused.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The location where vesicles resided on the ribbon when they fused can be determined using the two-color laser scanning method.
source: Since the positions of the ribbon and a labeled vesicle were known accurately, we were able to detect vesicle movements on the ribbon prior to fusion and determine where vesicles resided on the ribbon when they fused.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The experiments in this study complement and significantly extend previous studies based on TIRFM.
source: Therefore, our experiments complement and significantly extend the previous studies based on TIRFM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of methods and results with previous TIRFM studies.

claim: Synaptic vesicles bearing Vglut1-paRFP participated normally in the vesicle cycle.
source: Synaptic vesicles bearing Vglut1-paRFP participated normally in the vesicle cycle, since they were labeled by activity-dependent uptake of FM dye.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing FM dye uptake by Vglut1-paRFP labeled vesicles.

claim: Both mobile and immobile vesicles were visible after photoactivation.
source: Both mobile and immobile vesicles were visible after photoactivation (Video 1), but the immobile vesicles were closely associated with ribbons (Figure 1A,F; Video 2), which were labeled with green-fluorescent RBP introduced via a whole-cell patch pipette.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the video and figure data presented.

claim: Immobile vesicles were closely associated with ribbons.
source: Both mobile and immobile vesicles were visible after photoactivation (Video 1), but the immobile vesicles were closely associated with ribbons (Figure 1A,F; Video 2), which were labeled with green-fluorescent RBP introduced via a whole-cell patch pipette.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the video and figure data presented.

claim: Ribbon-associated vesicles are immobile because they are tethered to or near the ribbon itself.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the ribbon-associated vesicles are immobile because they are tethered to or near the ribbon itself (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that immobile vesicles are closely associated with ribbons.

claim: Immobile vesicles observed in this study likely correspond to the 'resident' vesicles observed at BPC active zones using TIRFM.
source: These immobile vesicles likely correspond to the 'resident' vesicles observed at BPC active zones using TIRFM (Zenisek et al., 2000; Midorikawa et al., 2007), except that our laser-scanning method detected vesicles located everywhere on the ribbon instead of only in a region <100 nm from the plasma membrane (the region marked with pink shading for illustrative purposes in Figure 1F).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with previous TIRFM studies and supported by citations.

claim: The laser-scanning method detected vesicles located everywhere on the ribbon instead of only in a region <100 nm from the plasma membrane.
source: These immobile vesicles likely correspond to the 'resident' vesicles observed at BPC active zones using TIRFM (Zenisek et al., 2000; Midorikawa et al., 2007), except that our laser-scanning method detected vesicles located everywhere on the ribbon instead of only in a region <100 nm from the plasma membrane (the region marked with pink shading for illustrative purposes in Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 1F showing vesicle positions across the full extent of the ribbon.

claim: Resident vesicles at ribbons move very little in the absence of stimulation.
source: Resident vesicles at ribbons move very little in the absence of stimulation (Zenisek, 2008), and we therefore used the temporal jitter in the observed position of paRFP-labeled vesicles relative to ribbons to estimate the spatial precision of the localization method under our imaging conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and used as a basis for estimating spatial precision.

claim: The vesicle position estimated by fitting 2D-Gaussians varied little during 90-s imaging periods, within ranges that averaged 27 nm on the x-axis and 17 nm on the y-axis.
source: The vesicle position estimated in this manner varied little during the 90-s imaging period (Figure 1G–I), within ranges that averaged 27 nm on the x-axis and 17 nm on the y-axis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 1G-I.

claim: The observed variation in estimated vesicle position is attributed to imaging noise that limits the spatial resolution.
source: Assuming that vesicles actually did not move during the imaging, we attribute the observed variation in estimated position to imaging noise that limits the spatial resolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the assumption that vesicles do not move in the absence of stimulation.

claim: Genuine stimulus-induced vesicle movements on the ribbon of approximately a vesicle diameter would be resolvable by comparing averaged x-y images before and after stimulation.
source: Therefore, genuine stimulus-induced vesicle movements on the ribbon of approximately a vesicle diameter would be resolvable by comparing averaged x-y images before and after stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured spatial precision of the method.

claim: BPCs exhibit two kinetically distinct components of transmitter release during depolarization: a fast component depleted within 10 ms, and a slower component lasting hundreds of ms.
source: BPCs exhibit two kinetically distinct components of transmitter release during depolarization (for zebrafish BPCs, see Vaithianathan and Matthews, 2014): a fast component depleted within 10 ms, and a slower component lasting hundreds of ms.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on zebrafish BPCs.

claim: The fast component of release is thought to represent the cohort of vesicles tethered to the ribbon nearest the plasma membrane.
source: We first determined how individual paRFP-labeled vesicles at the ribbon responded when the system was perturbed by releasing just the fast component, which is thought to represent the cohort of vesicles tethered to the ribbon nearest the plasma membrane (Matthews and Fuchs, 2010), where voltage-gated calcium channels reside.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and represents established knowledge about ribbon synapses.

claim: Voltage-gated calcium channels reside near the plasma membrane at the ribbon.
source: We first determined how individual paRFP-labeled vesicles at the ribbon responded when the system was perturbed by releasing just the fast component, which is thought to represent the cohort of vesicles tethered to the ribbon nearest the plasma membrane (Matthews and Fuchs, 2010), where voltage-gated calcium channels reside.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the localization of calcium channels at ribbon synapses.

claim: On some trials after a 10-ms stimulus, a new stable paRFP spot appeared at the ribbon.
source: On some trials after a 10-ms stimulus, a new stable paRFP spot appeared at the ribbon (Figure 2A,C), while on other trials, a previously present paRFP spot disappeared after the stimulus (Figure 2B,D), representing single-vesicle replenishment and loss, respectively.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2A,C.

claim: On some trials after a 10-ms stimulus, a previously present paRFP spot disappeared after the stimulus.
source: On some trials after a 10-ms stimulus, a new stable paRFP spot appeared at the ribbon (Figure 2A,C), while on other trials, a previously present paRFP spot disappeared after the stimulus (Figure 2B,D), representing single-vesicle replenishment and loss, respectively.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2B,D.

claim: Disappearances of paRFP spots clustered significantly closer to the plasma membrane than appearances along the axis perpendicular to the membrane.
source: However, disappearances clustered significantly closer to the plasma membrane than appearances (Figure 2E) along the axis perpendicular to the membrane (the x-axis; p<10-8, Wilcoxon rank test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2E and statistical analysis.

claim: There was no difference in the distribution of appearances and disappearances along the axis parallel to the membrane.
source: When the loci of gained and lost paRFP spots were determined as illustrated in Figure 1 and plotted with respect to the center of the ribbon (Figure 2E), there was no difference in the distribution of appearances and disappearances along the axis parallel to the membrane (the y-axis; p = 0.4, Wilcoxon rank test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2E and statistical analysis.

claim: The pattern revealed by single-vesicle imaging is consistent with selective fusion of membrane-proximal synaptic vesicles during brief depolarization.
source: This pattern revealed by single-vesicle imaging is consistent with selective fusion of membrane-proximal synaptic vesicles during brief depolarization, but preferential recruitment of new vesicles at the opposite pole of the ribbon to replace those lost, as suggested previously from population behavior of vesicles labeled with FM dye (Vaithianathan and Matthews, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed pattern of vesicle disappearances and appearances, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: New vesicles are preferentially recruited at the opposite pole of the ribbon to replace those lost during brief depolarization.
source: This pattern revealed by single-vesicle imaging is consistent with selective fusion of membrane-proximal synaptic vesicles during brief depolarization, but preferential recruitment of new vesicles at the opposite pole of the ribbon to replace those lost, as suggested previously from population behavior of vesicles labeled with FM dye (Vaithianathan and Matthews, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed pattern of vesicle appearances and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Loss of membrane-proximal vesicles creates the opportunity for vesicles remaining on the ribbon to rearrange and occupy the vacated region, opening up 'slots' for new vesicles at more distal positions on the ribbon.
source: A simple interpretation is that loss of membrane-proximal vesicles creates the opportunity for vesicles remaining on the ribbon to rearrange and occupy the vacated region, opening up 'slots' for new vesicles at more distal positions on the ribbon.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed pattern of vesicle turnover.

claim: After 10-ms stimulation, displacements of paRFP-labeled vesicles were larger than in the absence of stimulation.
source: However, after 10-ms stimulation, displacements were larger (Figure 2F; p≈0, Wilcoxon rank test), which is consistent with the prediction that the loss of ribbon-associated vesicles allows movement of remaining vesicles.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2F and statistical analysis.

claim: The larger displacements after stimulation are consistent with the prediction that the loss of ribbon-associated vesicles allows movement of remaining vesicles.
source: However, after 10-ms stimulation, displacements were larger (Figure 2F; p≈0, Wilcoxon rank test), which is consistent with the prediction that the loss of ribbon-associated vesicles allows movement of remaining vesicles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in displacement after stimulation.

claim: Without stimulation, 93% of displacement vectors were <50 nm.
source: Without stimulation (Figure 2G), vector amplitudes were mostly within the range expected for imaging noise (93% were <50 nm; see inset in Figure 2G for an expanded view to better reveal the large number of small vectors), and the direction of the vector was equally likely to be toward or away from the membrane (positive and negative ΔΔx, respectively, indicated by green and red vectors in Figure 2G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2G.

claim: Without stimulation, the direction of vesicle displacement was equally likely to be toward or away from the membrane.
source: Without stimulation (Figure 2G), vector amplitudes were mostly within the range expected for imaging noise (93% were <50 nm; see inset in Figure 2G for an expanded view to better reveal the large number of small vectors), and the direction of the vector was equally likely to be toward or away from the membrane (positive and negative ΔΔx, respectively, indicated by green and red vectors in Figure 2G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2G.

claim: After 10-ms stimuli, 77% of displacement vectors were >50 nm.
source: After 10-ms stimuli (Figure 2H), vector amplitudes were significantly larger (77% were >50 nm; p<10-6, Wilcoxon rank test), and there was a significant tendency for movement toward the membrane, with 70% of vectors having a positive ΔΔx (p=0.0008 that + and – ΔΔx were equally likely, by sign test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2H and statistical analysis.

claim: After 10-ms stimuli, there was a significant tendency for vesicle movement toward the membrane, with 70% of vectors having a positive ΔΔx.
source: After 10-ms stimuli (Figure 2H), vector amplitudes were significantly larger (77% were >50 nm; p<10-6, Wilcoxon rank test), and there was a significant tendency for movement toward the membrane, with 70% of vectors having a positive ΔΔx (p=0.0008 that + and – ΔΔx were equally likely, by sign test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2H and statistical analysis.

claim: Amplitudes of vectors both toward the membrane and away from the membrane were significantly larger after stimulation than in the absence of stimulation.
source: Amplitudes of vectors both toward the membrane (green vectors in Figure 2H) and away from the membrane (red vectors) were significantly larger after stimulation than in the absence of stimulation (+ΔΔx: 89 ± 8 nm vs. 17 ± 1 nm, p≈0, Wilcoxon rank test; -ΔΔx: 59 ± 6 nm vs. 16 ± 1 nm, p<10-12, Wilcoxon rank test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data and statistical analysis.

claim: The average vector after stimulation was a displacement by 33 nm toward the membrane, or approximately one vesicle diameter.
source: Overall, the average vector after stimulation (black arrow, Figure 2H) was a displacement by 33 nm toward the membrane, or approximately one vesicle diameter.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2H.

claim: The results suggest a mechanism of passive diffusion of tethered vesicles along the ribbon, such as the recently proposed 'crowd-surfing' model.
source: Since movements both toward and away from the plasma membrane were enhanced by stimulation, the results suggest a mechanism of passive diffusion of tethered vesicles along the ribbon, such as the recently proposed 'crowd-surfing' model (Graydon et al., 2014), rather than a directed motor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed bidirectional enhancement of movement, supported by citation to a proposed model.

claim: The net movement toward the membrane after stimulation is due to preferential release of vesicles near the membrane by 10-ms depolarization, creating the opportunity for more distal vesicles to diffuse into the vacated positions.
source: In such a passive mechanism, the net movement toward the membrane that we observed after stimulation is due to preferential release of vesicles near the membrane by 10-ms depolarization, creating the opportunity for more distal vesicles to diffuse into the vacated positions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed pattern of vesicle movements and the passive diffusion model.

claim: Ribbon synapses release neurotransmitter continuously during sustained depolarization in addition to the rapid burst of release at the onset of depolarization.
source: In addition to the rapid burst of release at the onset of depolarization, ribbon synapses also release neurotransmitter continuously during sustained depolarization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribbon synapse physiology.

claim: During sustained depolarization, previously stable paRFP spots often disappeared from the ribbon, either without a change in position before loss or after moving toward the membrane.
source: During sustained depolarization, previously stable paRFP spots often disappeared from the ribbon, either without a change in position before loss (e.g., Figure 4A) or after moving toward the membrane (e.g., Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Whether vesicles moved or not before disappearance depended on starting position with respect to the membrane.
source: Whether vesicles moved or not before disappearance depended on starting position with respect to the membrane (Figure 4D): vesicles nearer the plasma membrane (positive starting positions in Figure 4D) did not consistently move before disappearing, while distal vesicles (negative starting positions) moved toward the membrane before loss.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 4D.

claim: Vesicles nearer the plasma membrane did not consistently move before disappearing during sustained depolarization.
source: Whether vesicles moved or not before disappearance depended on starting position with respect to the membrane (Figure 4D): vesicles nearer the plasma membrane (positive starting positions in Figure 4D) did not consistently move before disappearing, while distal vesicles (negative starting positions) moved toward the membrane before loss.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 4D.

claim: Distal vesicles moved toward the membrane before loss during sustained depolarization.
source: Whether vesicles moved or not before disappearance depended on starting position with respect to the membrane (Figure 4D): vesicles nearer the plasma membrane (positive starting positions in Figure 4D) did not consistently move before disappearing, while distal vesicles (negative starting positions) moved toward the membrane before loss.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 4D.

claim: The histogram of final paRFP positions just prior to disappearance was broad and covered the full range of ribbon-associated vesicle positions.
source: Since membrane-proximal vesicles did not move while distal vesicles moved toward the ribbon center, the histogram of final paRFP positions just prior to disappearance was broad (Figure 4E) and covered the full range of ribbon-associated vesicle positions (cf., Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 4E.

claim: During disappearance, paRFP fluorescence did not cease abruptly, as would occur for bleaching, but instead declined along a Gaussian time course.
source: During disappearance, paRFP fluorescence did not cease abruptly, as would occur for bleaching, but instead declined along a Gaussian time course, which is consistent with diffusion of the emitter away from the scanned region (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Gaussian decline of paRFP fluorescence is consistent with diffusion of the emitter away from the scanned region.
source: During disappearance, paRFP fluorescence did not cease abruptly, as would occur for bleaching, but instead declined along a Gaussian time course, which is consistent with diffusion of the emitter away from the scanned region (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed time course of fluorescence decline.

claim: It is uncertain whether the diffusion of paRFP reflects movement of the Vglut1-paRFP protein itself or dissociation of an intact vesicle from the ribbon.
source: It is uncertain at present whether this diffusion reflects movement of the Vglut1-paRFP protein itself, as would occur for example if the protein incorporated into the plasma membrane after vesicle fusion, or dissociation of an intact vesicle from the ribbon.
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the interpretation of the observed diffusion.

claim: Unitary pHluorin events representing vesicle fusion were observed in x-t raster plots during sustained depolarizing voltage-clamp steps from -60 to -15 mV for 500–5000 ms.
source: Under these conditions, unitary pHluorin events representing vesicle fusion were observed in x-t raster plots during sustained depolarizing voltage-clamp steps from -60 to -15 mV for 500–5000 ms (Figure 5A,B), but not in the absence of stimulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 5A,B.

claim: pHluorin events were not observed in the absence of stimulation.
source: Under these conditions, unitary pHluorin events representing vesicle fusion were observed in x-t raster plots during sustained depolarizing voltage-clamp steps from -60 to -15 mV for 500–5000 ms (Figure 5A,B), but not in the absence of stimulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the absence of events in control conditions.

claim: pHluorin events sometimes arose near the plasma membrane, suggesting fusion of membrane-proximal vesicles.
source: Events sometimes arose near the plasma membrane, suggesting fusion of membrane-proximal vesicles (e.g., Figure 5C), but events also commonly originated at the distal pole of the ribbon, at a distance from the plasma membrane (e.g., Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 5C and represents an inference about the meaning of these events.

claim: pHluorin events commonly originated at the distal pole of the ribbon, at a distance from the plasma membrane.
source: Events sometimes arose near the plasma membrane, suggesting fusion of membrane-proximal vesicles (e.g., Figure 5C), but events also commonly originated at the distal pole of the ribbon, at a distance from the plasma membrane (e.g., Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 5D.

claim: pHluorin signals were broadly spread across the ribbon and were not confined to positions near the plasma membrane.
source: The histogram of event positions relative to the center of the ribbon (Figure 5E) showed that pHluorin signals were broadly spread across the ribbon (Figure 5E) and were not confined to positions near the plasma membrane, as would be expected if vesicles must first approach the plasma membrane in order to fuse.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 5E.

claim: The majority of pHluorin events arose at a substantial distance from the estimated membrane position, even after correcting for z-axis curvature.
source: However, the majority of pHluorin events still arose at a substantial distance from the estimated membrane position, even after correcting for z-axis curvature (dashed arrow, Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 5E after correction for membrane curvature.

claim: The estimated x-axis position of ribbons varied by less than ± 50 nm throughout the central part of the sampled z-axis range.
source: However, the estimated x-axis position of the ribbon varied by less than ± 50 nm throughout the central part of the sampled z-axis range (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The observed uncertainty in the x-axis position of ribbons within the optical section is insufficient to account for the wide range of pHluorin-event locations.
source: Therefore, the observed uncertainty in the x-axis position of ribbons within the optical section is insufficient to account for the wide range of pHluorin-event locations (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the ribbon position uncertainty with the range of pHluorin event positions.

claim: pHluorin events associated with ribbons arose both near the membrane and at more distal locations, at a substantial distance from the membrane.
source: We conclude that pHluorin events associated with ribbons arose both near the membrane and at more distal locations, at a substantial distance from the membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing the distribution of pHluorin event positions.

claim: A simple explanation for distal pHluorin events is that they represent fusion of synaptic vesicles with other ribbon-attached vesicles, which have themselves already undergone exocytosis and provide a path to the extracellular space.
source: A simple explanation is that the distal pHluorin events represent fusion of synaptic vesicles with other ribbon-attached vesicles, which have themselves already undergone exocytosis and provide a path to the extracellular space.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the distal pHluorin events.

claim: This model is consistent with previous work using electron microscopy, which suggested the existence of vesicle-vesicle compound fusion at ribbon synapses of goldfish BPCs.
source: This model is also consistent with previous work using electron microscopy (Matthews and Sterling, 2008), which suggested the existence of such vesicle-vesicle compound fusion at ribbon synapses of goldfish BPCs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous electron microscopy work.

claim: Prior studies of synaptic vesicle trafficking at BPC ribbon synapses using TIRFM focused on a narrow region extending ~100 nm from the plasma membrane and revealed vesicle movements within this region, as well as vesicle exocytosis at the membrane.
source: Prior studies of synaptic vesicle trafficking at BPC ribbon synapses using TIRFM focused on a narrow region extending ~100 nm from the plasma membrane and revealed vesicle movements within this region, as well as vesicle exocytosis at the membrane (Zenisek et al., 2000, 2002; Holt et al., 2004; Midorikawa et al., 2007; Zenisek, 2008).
evidence: This is a summary of previous TIRFM studies supported by citations.

claim: The imaging approaches in this study allowed vesicle motion and fusion to be detected across the entire population of ribbon-associated vesicles.
source: By contrast, our imaging approaches allowed vesicle motion and fusion to be detected across the entire population of ribbon-associated vesicles, albeit at a spatial resolution insufficient for detection of small movements of less than a vesicle diameter, like those reported in TIRFM experiments (Zenisek et al., 2000).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data showing vesicle positions and movements across the full extent of the ribbon.

claim: The spatial resolution of the imaging approach in this study was insufficient for detection of small movements of less than a vesicle diameter.
source: By contrast, our imaging approaches allowed vesicle motion and fusion to be detected across the entire population of ribbon-associated vesicles, albeit at a spatial resolution insufficient for detection of small movements of less than a vesicle diameter, like those reported in TIRFM experiments (Zenisek et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the method used in this study.

claim: The studies in this manuscript target a different set of questions and provide results that are complementary to the previous studies of synaptic vesicle dynamics at ribbon active zones.
source: Therefore, our studies target a different set of questions and provide results that are complementary to the previous studies of synaptic vesicle dynamics at ribbon active zones.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the methods and results with previous studies.

claim: The results suggest a dual role for the synaptic ribbon in neurotransmitter release at the active zone, with the ribbon serving as both a conduit for diffusion of tethered synaptic vesicles and a platform for vesicles to fuse distal to the plasma membrane.
source: Our results suggest a dual role for the synaptic ribbon in neurotransmitter release at the active zone, with the ribbon serving as both a conduit for diffusion of tethered synaptic vesicles and a platform for vesicles to fuse distal to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing vesicle diffusion and distal fusion events.
